blocks.text: DR JOHN GIBBS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could we, for the recording, start with your name?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: John Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You have given evidence before and you have come to assist us today with your dealings with a baby by the name of [Baby M] --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: -- back in April 2016. You have prepared a statement in this matter?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In that statement, by way of introduction, you reminded yourself that he was born on 8 April 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You noted that his Apgar scores were high and thus he was in good condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Because he was small and premature, he was admitted with his twin, [Baby L], to the neonatal unit at Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The purpose was to monitor and establish feeds?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it right that on the first day of [Baby M]'s life his blood was taken to check for infection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And that subsequently that blood did not reveal any bacterial infection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it right that his C-reactive protein, one of the indicators of infection, as we've heard, was less than 1 during the first day of life and indeed the next few days?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, and it's not just an indication of infection, it's also an indication of any inflammation in the body and it indicated neither of those were likely to be present.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. We have heard of events on the afternoon of 9 April 2016 when [Baby M] was attended by Doctors Ukoh and Jayaram as a consequence of a collapse that day. Is it right that you first met [Baby M] at 9.35 am on 10 April 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Which would be his third day of life?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And you took a note of your examination of [Baby M] on that occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I wonder if we could go to that note, please. Tile 348, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Would you wish to refresh your memory from the note before we go through it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: (Pause)

We have not only heard about the events of the preceding day, we've also heard about some treatment that [Baby M] received through the early hours of the morning on 10 April. Would you have familiarised yourself with that from the notes before you examined him?

Yes. Partly from the notes and partly because we always have handover at about 8.30 in the morning of all the patients on the neonatal unit, so I would have been told a summary of what had happened to him the previous afternoon and during the night.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. We've heard from a [Dr A] who treated him on the 9th. Does that accord with your recollection of the handover?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was it with [Dr A] you spoke before you examined [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He would have led the handover, yes. This is the Sunday morning, yes, about 8.30.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we could then look at your note, you begin with the age and the corrected age.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then if you could take us through your note.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The problems for [Baby M] when I saw him on the Sunday morning at about 9.35 -- the main problem was he'd had a cardiorespiratory arrest on the previous day, that was in the afternoon. I put down "query septic", was it probably due to infection, or "query NEC", necrotising enterocolitis. But it subsequently transpired he didn't have either of those, so there was no proper explanation for his cardiorespiratory arrest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then the second problem, he's the second of two twins, and that DCDA just means they were just likely, but not definite, to be non-identical twins.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Number 3, he had born by lower segment caesarean section, and caesarean section because of IUGR, intrauterine growth retardation in the first twin, that's his twin, [Baby L].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then he'd also, number 4, become jaundiced on the first day of life and we call that early jaundice because jaundice in premature babies is not uncommon by 3 or 4 days of age, less common in the first day of life.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then number 5, he'd been suffering from recurrent brief -- and I originally wrote "apnoea", crossed it out and initialled it above. Apnoea would mean he stops breathing but I decided it was more accurate to say bradyapnoea, abnormally slow breathing, with oxygen desaturations, desats, and that "brady" there means slowing of the heart rate, bradycardia.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. So slowing but not stopping, that being the distinction?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Most of the time, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You have then noted the drugs that he was receiving?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, those are three different antibiotics he was on at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then fluids. Intravenous?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, intravenous and that's the volume, 90ml per kilogram per day of TPN, total parenteral nutrition.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He was not receiving anything by mouth at the moment while he was recovering from his cardiorespiratory arrest the previous afternoon.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We have heard that he went nil by mouth shortly before that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct. He was still nil by mouth on the Sunday morning.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that on examination?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Well, actually, probably just -- it's meant to be just before on examination. I have inserted a line:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Minimal bili [that's bile stains] nasogastric aspirates overnight."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then I put "on examination", and then I record my findings on examining [Baby M]. So he was quiet, and by quiet he's only a little baby, 3 days old, a 33-week premature baby. By quiet I just meant he was not moving much at all, not just not making sounds.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: He was receiving CPAP support for his breathing. So he's breathing by himself but with a little extra pressure to help keep his lungs open and he was needing a modest amount of oxygen, 26% rather than the normal 21% that's in air. And the pressure of the CPAP, I have just recorded it for information, was 6.5 centimetres of water.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can I just interrupt for a moment, we heard yesterday that overnight his ventilation had moved from mechanical ventilation, intubation, he had then been extubated, he'd gone from BiPAP to CPAP. Does that tell you anything with your experience?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It meant he was needing less support progressively with his breathing, so from that point of view he was improving, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The next note, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He had clear -- that's -- the "BS" is breath sounds. So listening to his chest, it was clear on both sides.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Heart sounds were normal. That's the first and second heart sound plus nil, meaning no murmurs. Then I've written he had a soft abdomen and it was not tender.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we can scroll down a little bit. You've set out a plan in light of your notes and examination.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The plan was to add caffeine, but I've written an explanation for that. His carbon dioxide levels on his blood gases were moderately increased. That's the upper arrow. And I have put in brackets "in the 7s".
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Normally they should be up to about 6.5, so it's an increase in his carbon dioxide levels, with a corresponding drop in his pH, meaning he was a little bit acidotic and I put in brackets 7.25. That's acceptable but we generally don't like to allow the pH to drop much below 7.25.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And because of the fact he was having episodes of bradyapnoea, slowing of his breathing, in fact looking at his observation chart, his breathing level was relatively slow for a premature baby and the fact that his carbon dioxide level was slightly elevated, meaning he wasn't quite breathing enough, I felt we should add caffeine, which is a respiratory stimulant, it helps to stimulate breathing in premature babies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then to continue with the ABs, the antibiotics, and remain NBM, nil by mouth. And then to repeat some blood tests, a further CRP, full blood count and U&Es.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That CRP and full blood count showed no increase in the CRP level, no increase in the white cell count, so all remaining normal and making it unlikely he was suffering from infection or NEC.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We see then your signature. Is that the conclusion of that particular examination?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, at that time.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We can see that there follows, fairly soon after, another note. Were you asked to review [Baby M] shortly after you'd finished that examination?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. And from memory, in between those two, in the 40 minutes in between, I'd seen his brother, [Baby L]. So I was still with the twins but I had moved on to [Baby L], when something happened to [Baby M] and I was called back to him.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So you'd looked at [Baby L] for about 40 minutes or so. Do you remember who asked you to look again at [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember exactly. It was likely to be the nurse looking after him and I know from the notes who that nurse was.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We heard a statement yesterday, I think, from Laura Eagles; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, that's the nurse who's recorded in the notes, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What did you find when you asked -- what were you told first and then what did you find?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, at that time, [Baby M] had recovered because Staff Nurse Eagles had provided some support for his breathing, but his breathing had slowed down again, that's bradyapnoea, going to briefly stopping breathing, that's the apnoea, and the oxygen level had dropped to 60% instead of remaining above 90%.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And at the end of that line I put:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Not responding to tactile stimulation..."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's stroking or flicking [Baby M]'s feet. That was being done by the nurse, I didn't do that:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Not responding to tactile stimulation and increased facial oxygen."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the oxygen was turned up from the 26% to between 60% and 100%. But he didn't respond to that, but he did then respond to being Neopuffed, so giving him some ventilation breaths just through a mask on his face.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That was for about 90 seconds.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The plan I made before that that we've already referred to was to give caffeine. It hadn't been given by this stage, so given that [Baby M] was continuing to have slowing of his breathing, I felt it was time to make sure the caffeine was given as soon as possible to stimulate his breathing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll come to that in a moment. From your notes, what you found, the treatment that he received, what concerns would that raise?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, the concern was that although he was recovering from the need for full ventilation, he was still needing stimulation intermittently because his breathing was slowing down, and therefore we needed to give him more help, in addition to continuing antibiotics for any infection that might have been
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: there that we never proved, but he needed some extra help with his breathing.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You mentioned the caffeine. If I can ask Mr Murphy, please, to go to the next tile, 354. We probably don't need to go behind it. We can see that the caffeine was then administered at 10.31. That would be following on from your instruction at 10.15?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: After the caffeine and in the days that followed, are you aware whether [Baby M] continued to suffer with any breathing difficulties?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't believe he did. I didn't see him every day after that, but looking at his observation charts, the caffeine coincided with an improvement in that he didn't have episodes where he needed stimulation for his breathing after that, as recorded by the nurses.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was his breathing support escalated in any way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. I think it was a couple of days later he managed without the CPAP and then, I can't remember exactly when, the additional oxygen was no longer needed. So he did steadily improve after that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So his breathing continued in the same trajectory as in the morning of the 10th and in the days that followed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, but with the change being the episodes where he would slow or sometimes stop his breathing stopped after the caffeine had been given.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did the antibiotics continue?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They did whilst waiting for the blood cultures and then were stopped some days later when the cultures were negative and yet again there had been -- over 48 to 72 hours after the time I saw [Baby M], his white cell count and his CRP remained normal, indicating it was unlikely he was suffering from an infection.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So no evidence of an infection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Was an X-ray taken of [Baby M] at the time?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Various X-rays were taken from [Baby M], the first one being after his cardiorespiratory arrest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Were you able to look at those X-rays whilst treating him?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What did they tell you about the collapse that had occurred on 9 April?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, to me, they did not provide any explanation. In particular, his lung fields were clear on those X-rays -- the Xrays taken, I think, an hour after the first one, an hour after his cardiorespiratory arrest had begun, showed clear. Subsequent X-rays were mainly taken to look at various lines that were inserted to him over the next -- into him over the next few days.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Any evidence on those X-rays of what we've heard of as NEC or necrotising enterocolitis?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did the investigation, if I can put it that way, extend to a heart scan?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that an ultrasound scan undertaken by your colleague, Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, Dr Brearey, I think on the 13th. It was a couple of days after I'd seen [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Did that ultrasound scan of the heart reveal any explanation for events on 9 April?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. The reason I hesitate is that Dr Brearey thought, looking at the comments he made in the notes, there might have been a thrombus in one of the chambers of the heart but on review a few days later it was normal, and on discussion with the heart specialist in Liverpool, their view was probably it was a variation of normal that he'd seen and not a thrombus in the heart. If there'd been thrombus in the heart, it would be very uncertain whether that had caused any cardiorespiratory arrest or in fact the result of the heart having stopped for a period of time, so whether it was cause or effect from the cardiorespiratory arrest. But the overall conclusion, and Dr Brearey would be able to tell the court more, was that probably the scan was completely normal.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In fact, we will hear from the consultant who he spoke to, so thank you for the introduction. How would you characterise [Baby M]'s recovery from the event on 9 April?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He made a steady recovery, but when I saw him on that morning of the 10th, he still wasn't behaving normally in that he was quiet and his breathing was slow. But that's explicable for a child who had very nearly died the previous afternoon. So it could have been a consequence of that that he wasn't behaving normally and had some breathing difficulties. And also, it could be partly the consequence of all the medication he'd required to be mechanically ventilated for 10 hours or so after the cardiorespiratory arrest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Did [Baby M]'s recovery continue to the extent that he was discharged about 3.5 weeks later?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So he did make a good recovery and, in particular, managed to get back on to feeds and was feeding well by the time he was discharged, which is an encouraging sign for a premature baby.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. I have no more questions for you, Dr Gibbs. Thank you. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: We have no questions, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you, Mr Myers. I have no questions either. Thank you, Dr Gibbs, for coming back and giving evidence this morning. You will be giving evidence again I see from the list, so what I have said to you before still applies: no conversation with anyone about anything to do with this case. Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
My Lord, Minna Lappalainen, please.

Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Could we start with your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My full name is Minna (inaudible) Lappalainen.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: Even though I'm asking the questions, and I know it's very artificial, could I ask you to keep your voice up, please, so that the ladies and gentlemen at the back of the room can hear you clearly.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay. Can you hear me? Yes?
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: Thank you. Your occupation, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm a retired senior neonatal nurse.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: Were you employed in that capacity at the neonatal unit at Chester in 2016?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: You've been reminded that in that capacity, you were working a night shift on the neonatal unit between the 8th and 9 April 2016; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: We've heard about various bands of nurses, the banding process. What band would you have been considered that particular night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: Thank you. I think you have seen the notes from your night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: And you were able to confirm that you were not the designated nurse for a baby called [Baby L]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: And you were able to check the notes. Can you confirm whether or not insulin was prescribed for [Baby L] on that particular night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: Did you counter-check any insulin prescription or otherwise that particular night?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: And did you administer insulin to [Baby L] during that night shift?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No questions, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you, nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: We anticipate we will hear from Nurse Lappalainen again.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That completes your evidence at this stage. Thank you very much for coming this morning and giving evidence. You will, I gather, be required again later on in the trial. You'll be told when that is, obviously. In the meantime please don't talk to anyone about anything to do with this case, any of the babies or anything to do with it. All right?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: LAPPALAINEN

blocks.text: Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Right. I think we've discussed how babies who are on intravenous fluids, the fluids are given through a pump, which regulates the volume accurately, and the pump also has a feature so that if there's any air in the plastic tubing, the pump will alarm and stop. But from the end of this pump to the cannula that goes into the baby, there is still a fair bit of plastic tubing that contains fluid.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: In addition to that, one normally attaches some form of tap so that it's possible for babies to receive fluid but also if you need to give them antibiotics or some other substance, you can give an injection of antibiotics or fluid without disrupting the continuity of the plastic tubing. blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: ensures that no air can get into the circulation, no air can get into the fluid accidentally.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, if there was any air in that syringe, that air would then get into what we call the dead space, in other words the bit of tubing between the bung and the end of the cannula that connects to the baby.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think his collapse was due to an air embolus. I think his collapse was due to air being administered to him some time before 16.02. blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The second problem we have is because of the care that nurses and doctors take in the management of babies on intravenous fluids and the sophistication of the equipment used, accidental air injection is virtually unheard of. blocks.text: This isn't dealing with the question I asked.

blocks.text: The other place the baby's air will go to is into the left side of the heart and this is where you have a difference between the effects of air embolus in a baby compared to the effect of air embolus in an older child or adult because the baby has, in simple terms, a hole in the heart, a hole between the right side of the heart and the left side of the heart this. blocks.text: If air gets from the right side of the heart into the left side of the heart, then where it goes after that depends on a number of factors, but it will dissipate. So if it gets into the blood vessels supplying the abdomen, you'll get this discolouration.

blocks.text: "I am Stavros Michael Stivaros. My specialist field is paediatric neuroradiology. I am the lead consultant paediatric neuroradiologist at Royal Manchester Children's Hospital.

blocks.text: He then sets out the references for the images and other material that he has considered:
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Baby M] had an MRI scan of his brain performed on 27 May 2016 at the Countess of Chester Hospital.

blocks.text: "Brain appearances: the brain appearances are abnormal. I think that it is likely that the cause of these imaging findings is the cardiorespiratory collapse suffered by [Baby M] on 9 April 2016. However, the imaging can only describe the brain damage
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: resultant from this episode. It cannot determine the underlying cause of the collapse, about which I defer to clinical opinion."

blocks.text: -- markings are 5 per degree. Is there a causal connection potentially between photo/light therapy and a raised temperature?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. When babies are under phototherapy they are usually put in an incubator to receive that kind of treatment because, particularly premature, babies are very small, they lose heat very rapidly. So when they receive phototherapy they're naked because you want the light to be exposed to as much of their skin as possible. They have some eye shields or goggles to protect their eyes from the ultraviolet light, but other than that they are naked. So other than they are put in an incubator which is heated but the very fact that they've got ultraviolet
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: lights, usually above the incubator, means that they quite often get hot, so it's not uncommon for them to get a slight temperature and the nursing staff to have to alter the temperature of the incubator to allow for that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Also, when babies get hot they tend to breathe a bit quicker, so their work of breathing may well increase during that time. Either their rate of breathing or just their work of breathing may increase because they're hot, and this temperature was very -- was still in the normal range in fact, but the nurse did absolutely the right thing and reduced the incubator temperature by half a degree and thereafter the temperature settled.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. So that's [Baby M]'s position immediately before his collapse. You note at your paragraph 7.5 that a new bag of dextrose was started at about 3.30.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that he was given benzylpenicillin, which is an antibiotic; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: At a time which was noted as being 15.45?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That was what was noted in the notes, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can you tell us what happened thereafter, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, as far as the notes tell me, he was given the antibiotics at 15.45. But at just after 4 o'clock, he stopped breathing suddenly and became very bradycardic, so his heart rate fell dramatically and that was associated with a desaturation. This led to the team giving him prolonged and sustained resuscitation over a significant amount of time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He didn't respond initially to the usual things that one would do with resuscitation, so he then went on to require, in total, six doses of adrenaline and two doses of bicarbonate as well as being intubated. All of that took nearly half an hour, which is an extremely long time for a baby to be in cardiorespiratory arrest for.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They did eventually manage to get him to recover and it was noted that he began gasping and had a heart rate of over 100 at about 27 minutes after the cardiac arrest started.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We heard that he was ventilated in the sense of he was given -- put -- an ET tube was inserted; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. He was bagged initially with a Neopuff that we've heard about before and was receiving chest compressions, but when Dr Ukoh came, he intubated him and therefore he had a more secure airway and that was at around between 10 and 11 minutes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. We've heard about the blood gas taken by [Nurse B], a printout from that. What did that show?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It was a very abnormal blood gas. But I would say it's quite unusual to take a blood gas in the middle of a resuscitation. I can only assume the clinical team decided to take this blood gas because at that stage [Baby M] had been resuscitated for quite some time without showing signs of improvement, and as we heard from the clinical team, they were considering stopping treatment.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So I think probably that the blood gas was taken so that they could see kind of how bad things were on the blood gas.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The difficulty is that this blood gas was taken from a capillary sample, which is done from a heel prick by a little needle jabbing into the baby's heel. And that's always going to be very abnormal if you're in the middle of a cardiac arrest. And also it is quite difficult to get the blood because the baby really has no circulation if the baby is receiving cardiac compressions.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So ideally, if you wanted to get a true picture of what was going on, you'd do an arterial sample, but this baby didn't have an arterial line, so they did the best they could, but it showed a very, very abnormal blood gas with a marked respiratory acidosis and a metabolic acidosis and showed a very high lactate, which indicates that the baby's metabolism was ongoing without oxygen for some time -- the lactate was in double figures, I think.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's in that -- it's actually 9.8.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it's very abnormal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That also, of course, gives you a reference point to compare to what happened after then when periodically blood gases were taken, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, he needed blood gases afterwards (a) to chart his recovery, but he was also receiving respiratory support.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So babies receiving any sort of respiratory support tend to get regular blood gases. The frequency of them depends on what sort of respiratory support they're on, so if they're on a lot of ventilation, they're extremely sick, they may get blood gases
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: every hour or so. When they're stable on CPAP, they might get blood gases twice a day. There is no set pattern. So he did need to have blood gases subsequently just to check his progress.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But if you're not on any respiratory support, you don't get any blood gases taken.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Just taking up the point to which Dr Evans was directed this morning about the hours leading up to [Baby M]'s collapse, would you agree with Dr Evans in that respect that because he wasn't on respiratory support and because there was no suggestion that he was going to become ill, you wouldn't expect the hospital to have taken blood gases?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. A baby of 33 weeks' gestation, so although premature, relatively mature for a premature baby, who was in air and was well, you wouldn't subject that baby to regular blood gases, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. So what did you think, looking at your paragraph 7.9 now, about the circumstances of [Baby M]'s collapse?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was concerned about the collapse because it was highly unusual. There were no clinical hints that he was about to have a sudden and catastrophic cardiorespiratory arrest. And that is unusual in premature infants and I've certainly said that before when giving evidence.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Premature infants who are unwell, you usually get some sort of hint that something is going on, which informs you that you need to keep a special watch on them, maybe screen for sepsis. There are very few things that cause a baby to collapse in this way and I considered some of those, although I felt that the clinical picture didn't fit with those, but I did consider things like infection because that's always a possibility in premature babies.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This didn't fit with an infection.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Aspiration is one thing, where milk feeds go down into the lungs rather than into the gut. But of course he was nil by mouth, so that was not a likely cause.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Necrotising enterocolitis, but again I felt that was unlikely as well. Electrolyte disturbance can sometimes cause a collapse, that wasn't the case here. And a congenital heart problem was the final thing that I excluded from my differential diagnosis because he didn't have a congenital heart problem and he was monitored and so there was no rhythm disturbance noted prior to his collapse. So this was completely unexpected.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the electrolyte disturbance was concerned, is that the electrolytes in the circulation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, blood electrolytes. Electrolytes are salts that are in the blood and they can be measured by sending samples to the laboratory or the main ones that we're concerned about in premature infants are -- you get a readout from the blood gas machine. So neonates of this age may get a once a day electrolyte problem (sic).
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There was no reason to suspect he should have one, his kidneys were working okay, so there was no reason to suspect an electrolyte problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is this the sodium and --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sodium and potassium.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So you had results for that and they failed to suggest that anything was abnormal?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct and he wasn't receiving additional sodium or potassium in any intravenous fluids.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So having, in your opinion, reasonably excluded the obvious possibilities, did you take anything else into account?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, my conclusion was that I had to find some way to explain that a baby who was previously well had suddenly collapsed, had a very prolonged cardiorespiratory arrest from which he almost did not recover, and then, within a very short space of time, appeared relatively stable again. And I could think of no other things that could cause that other than an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In that context we had some evidence from the treating medics that, on being ventilated, [Baby M]'s chest was rising, falling, the capnograph was registering CO2 coming out, and yet his sats were still dropping. Does that set of observations -is that consistent with the suggestion of an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, what that does is exclude a respiratory cause, so a breathing cause, for this collapse because if the clinical team can see his chest moving and then once he was intubated, could see that the breathing tube was in the correct place by the capnograph working, that means oxygen is delivered to his lungs yet we are still in a cardiac arrest state. So it excludes a respiratory cause and the only other cause I was left with was that of an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And so far as -- you have listened to all the evidence of those who treated [Baby M] during the material time; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And so far as that evidence -- taking it as a whole, is that consistent with your opinion?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I heard Dr Jayaram yesterday, who described the changes in skin discolouration and they are compatible with that of an air embolus and we've discussed that in other cases in this trial.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Later on in the preparations for this trial, you provided a witness statement dated 17 August; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That was last year I should have said. Were you asked in that context to consider the mechanism by which it would be possible for somebody with a malevolent intention to introduce air into the circulation of [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In considering that issue, what material did you take into account?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I was provided by some videos by the police, who had prepared these videos for Operation Hummingbird. And one of the videos was entitled "Cannulation", which showed the process of cannulation and the equipment used at the time at the Countess of Chester Hospital. Then the second video was titled "Infusion pumps", which showed how an infusion bag of fluid was set up using the Alaris volumetric pump that was in use at the time at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think we've seen these videos --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We have, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- in the course of the evidence, haven't we?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the cannulation -- I think we have seen the infusion pump video more than once, and the cannulation one, to bring it back to mind, it has a sort of -- it looks like one of those sort of hands from a joke shop almost.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it has an adult arm, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So putting that material together with your specialist knowledge of what goes on in these sorts of situations, what conclusions did you come to?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I concluded that there were three possible mechanisms whereby air could have been administered into [Baby M]'s line. The first was that air could have been injected into the bung on a T-piece. There was a photograph shown this morning by Mr Myers of a T-piece.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Let's just get the photograph up because it might help you if we can just -- if Mr Murphy wouldn't mind reminding us of what we saw (inaudible: off microphone).
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's the (inaudible: off microphone) report, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: It is. Once a IV cannula is put in, it is possible to attach the giving set directly to the end of the cannula, but in a baby where the cannula is really very small, the weight of the tubing of the giving set can pull the cannula and dislodge it. So it's absolutely standard practice to have an extra piece of tubing between the giving set and the cannula to prevent -- you tape it in a particular way to prevent the giving set tubing being dragged out and losing the cannula because they are not easy to place, so you don't want to keep replacing them.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the top piece of equipment is called a T-piece.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I was told by the police that this was the type of T-piece that was used at the Countess of Chester Hospital at the time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Could you show us --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Sorry, it wasn't working before. This is a T-piece (indicating). This bit (indicating) goes to the baby and this bit connects to the giving set of the intravenous infusion (indicating).
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: These connection tubes come in a variety -- there are a variety of makes, a variety of sizes. This is a rather old-fashioned one and I don't think they're made anymore, but I was told this was what was available at the Countess of Chester at the time. You can see it has this extra bung at the top there (indicating). This bit (indicating) attaches to the cannula, this bit(indicating) would be primed with saline before you attach it to the baby and this bit (indicating) could either have a bung on the end and be left with nothing attached to it or it could be attached to a giving set and fluid infused in it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In addition to that, if you want to be able to access the intravenous line to give antibiotics, rather than keep undoing this, if it's got fluid infusing through it, you can also put this within this mechanism so there would be this bit going to the baby, a T-piece here, this three-way tap attached there, and then the giving set attached on to that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This is also primed, but clearly all of this -- and this has a potential to be a dead space so you have to prime it with fluid before attaching it to the baby, otherwise it's full of air and that can cause a problem.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So my conclusions were that there were three possible ways where [Baby M] could have had air administered. Firstly, it could have been through this bung (indicating) because that was the kind of T-piece used at the time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just for the transcript, that's the yellow-coloured --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. It's a self-sealing rubber bung.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's what I was just going to ask you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: A bung means different things to different people.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's a self-sealing rubber bung.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A rubber bung. So in order to administer it, you do -- put what through the --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: A syringe, a needle through that. You'd have to do that in order to get anything, fluid or anything else, through there.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It's the same idea as what there is, as a matter of fact, on the top of a vial of insulin?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, exactly the same. Exactly the same.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The second way is if a three-way tap was in situ, and I'm not sure if they were in use at the time at the Countess of Chester, three-way taps would have been in use but I'm not sure if this was their standard way of administering IV fluids. I think it probably was fairly standard. Clearly, if this white bung on the three-way tap is attached there (indicating), and this blue bung is attached to the giving set giving intravenous fluid, this other bung can be used to give antibiotics, but also air could have been injected via that route as well.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sorry, just for the sake of completeness, how through that spare portal, I'll call it?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just with a syringe. You don't need a needle then because that is just open. Once that yellow one is removed, it's open. So you just screw a syringe on and then you can inject air, fluid, or whatever you need to inject. Usually antibiotics or other drugs are given via that route directly.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If no three-way tap was in place in this set-up, which I think would be unusual because [Baby M] was on antibiotics, air could have been injected using a syringe directly into this T-piece once the IV fluids had been disconnected. So at the time of administering antibiotics, if you haven't got a T-piece you'd have to undo the IV fluids and then give the antibiotics by attaching a syringe at that end and so obviously antibiotic, other fluids, or air could be administered in that way.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you consider the alternative factual scenarios of what would induce an almost immediate collapse of a baby and what might induce a delayed collapse?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, as I've said, in giving evidence before, the actual volume of air that causes a baby to collapse and die is unknown. But if a large volume of air was injected by whichever of the three means I've suggested -- if a large volume of air was injected, that would immediately cause some sort of air lock in the heart and the baby would have a cardiac arrest and die and would not be able to recover.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If the amount of air injected was of a smaller volume and was not injected as a big push but was in the dead space of this and then all of this was filled with air, which is a small volume, but the fluids were then reconnected, that would take some minutes to get to the baby because [Baby M] was only on, I think, 5.5ml an hour or 5.3ml an hour of fluids, which is 0.8ml per minute.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So a really, really -- very slow infusion and so if air was in these pieces of equipment it would take some minutes to actually get into the patient and get to the heart to cause the collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But because the volume was not sufficient to cause the air lock and cardiac arrest, it didn't cause a sudden death. It did cause an arrest, but something from which he was resuscitated from.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for you at this stage, thank you. If you'd wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And you enlarge upon that, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you exclude anything to do with aspiration by feeding?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I'd not seen Dr Jayaram's statement at that point or since.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think you said to the jury that when you considered all of this, the words you used were you had to find some way to explain the collapse in a baby who you say was stable.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But as a medical exercise and as an expert, Dr Bohin, it isn't inevitable that you have to reach for some explanation if no explanation is equally suitable?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, you don't make an explanation up. You look for a differential diagnosis of possible causes and then either confirm or exclude them, which is what I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sometimes there can be a cause, a medical cause, that is nevertheless unascertained, can't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't think of a situation where that would occur, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Does it not remain the case that one can't exclude the possibility of a medical explanation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think that is the explanation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What you've done is to look for some sort of explanation, some sort, and reached for air embolus, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The factors you rely on for air embolus or the fact, really, is the speed of the collapse and then the recovery; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it's not just that. It's the fact that the baby was well before, so this baby had a precipitous cardiac arrest and that is just incredibly unusual of babies of that gestation who were well beforehand. And babies who have an underlying cardiac cause or other cause, having been resuscitated, remain very, very unwell for some time and that is just not what we saw in this case. And air embolus fits with what the medical staff and the team on the ground at the time saw.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There is no specific evidence, as it happens, of an air embolus at all, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's no single diagnostic feature of an air embolus, but this clinical scenario fits with an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When you say, as you say in the report, "There were no physiological hints of him becoming unstable", again I'm not going to rehearse everything we've gone over through what happened in the day before the collapse. I am going to suggest there are actually, to use your word, hints that something wasn't right with [Baby M]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You don't accept that any of the material we have been through in terms of what the nurses identified and being made nil by mouth is any indication of being unwell?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I don't think he was unwell. I think he was under phototherapy, which made his hot, which made him breathe quicker. He had 1.5ml of bile-stained aspirates -- so I think we need to make it clear it wasn't pure bile, it was bile-stained aspirates, so gastric juice along with bile. That potentially may have been a problem. The medical (sic) staff did exactly the right thing by asking the doctor to review it and they were being very cautious and stopped his feeds. But as we found out, he did not have an underlying gastrointestinal cause for his collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Whatever the reason for there not being a blood gas check in the 22 or so hours between the last one and the collapse, as
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: a fact we cannot know what his blood gas was like over that period, can we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, no, because one wasn't taken and there was no clinical indication to take one.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You can't assume therefore everything where that is concerned is fine, can we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We only undertake blood tests on babies if we think they're unwell, to try and find out why they're unwell.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The medical team treating him clearly didn't think he was unwell or they would have undertaken some tests.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We don't do blood tests willy-nilly on babies. It's not appropriate, it's not ethical to do that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They thought there was potential problem enough for him to be made nil by mouth, didn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was a precautionary measure and the medics at the time decided to adopt a watch-and-wait approach, which is very common. If things had changed after that, they may have investigated further, but as it happened, things didn't change until he collapsed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Being made nil by mouth is a deviation from the norm, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not for a baby of that gestation. They are put on and off feeds on a very regular basis.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And one can't disregard the possibility that the collapse that happened at 16.00 is medically connected to what had happened before?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think it is, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As to what happens afterwards, we know there are bradycardias and desaturations in the 12 to 24 hours that followed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They could be linked to the collapse at 4 pm on the 9th, obviously?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: They could be linked to an underlying issue that plays a part in that collapse? That's a possibility, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think it unlikely given the description of the posturing that was given by the medical and nursing staff. The description of the posturing shows a baby who's suffered some sort of hypoxia in the clenching -- the sucking on the endotracheal tube and the posturing of his limbs is very characteristic of a baby who's suffered a hypoxic insult and, so far as I'm aware, there were no other hypoxic insults around that time.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: When we get to 10.15 on the 10th and there's bradyapnoea and apnoea and desaturating to 60, that isn't the time of the fist clenching or the sucking on the tube.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that could be part of an underlying issue as much as it could be a consequence of what had happened on the 9th at 4 pm?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I think it was a consequence of his collapse on the previous day.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can I confirm, are you able to discount entirely an underlying issue or is that possibility?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I think you can discount it because he didn't go on to have any other problems that you could relate to that time. So if he had an underlying issue it would have emerged and we would have known about it. He had no other underlying issue that emerged subsequently.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you accept that when one considers cause in a medical situation like this, there has to be consideration of the possibility of a medical cause that has not been identified?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There has to be consideration, but looking at the entire history, which is what I did, nothing else came out of the history or his clinical presentation which would lead me to think that there was an underlying cause which, up until the point of his collapse, had not been discovered. Not then, not since.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You settle on air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you do that principally because of the unexpected nature of a rapid collapse and then a recovery?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In a baby that was previously well and the findings of Dr Jayaram with the skin changes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can I just ask this -- oh, so you do rely on what Dr Jayaram says there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I had to take that into consideration.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. That forms part of your basis for the conclusion that it is an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I want to move next to the question of mechanism. When you've considered how this could happen, you've relied upon material provided to you by the police; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You've listened to the evidence over the past few days.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's not actually been a description from any member of staff as to the precise set-up of this kit, has there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you have no information directly from anyone who's working there as to the use of three-way taps at the Countess of Chester, have you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. As I said, it would be standard practice. If a baby was receiving intravenous fluids and having antibiotics and only had one line, it would be standard practice to have a three-way tap in situ because what you don't want to do is to keep unlocking the fluids and have to inject antibiotics and then out the fluids back on because that poses an infection risk. So I would say although I don't know for absolutely sure, it is absolutely standard in every hospital I've worked at for a three-way tap or a similar device -- now we have something called an octopus -- to be in place to allow multiple ports.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That's what I was going to ask you actually. There is an alternative which is an octopus connection, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There is an alternative. I asked -- I am not quite sure when octopus devices came in. When I asked the police what was in use by the Countess of Chester at the time, I was given a picture of that T-piece, which is a fairly old-fashioned device and we don't use them anymore. Now we would use an octopus
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: device and I believe the Countess of Chester do use octopus devices now but when that was brought in, I don't know.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Just to assist anyone who isn't immediately up on what an octopus is, that's the connection with possibly any number of little tubes coming off it individually that hang loose?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. So whereas that T-piece that I showed just had one arm, an octopus can have two, three, four or more.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that's how you deal with the question of needing multiple ports, you use a different arm for different entries?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If we carry on with the T-piece that you were provided with just to confirm some issues relating to that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You've described the three possible ways that air could be introduced with the T-piece and three-way tap set-up that you have given us.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You accept, Dr Bohin, it's simply not possible to provide an accurate timescale as to how quickly air would travel and how quickly collapse would follow; that's right, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You can't do that. You agree, don't you, that rapid injection of a volume of air into any of those three points could cause an almost immediate collapse?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A large volume of air, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: By large, we're talking maybe a millilitre?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Millilitres, yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As we heard earlier, the bore of these tubes is very narrow, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If you squeeze a little bit in, it's going to travel quickly.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It depends how strongly you push it, I suppose.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: All right. But we have seen also with the insulin infusions during the resuscitation, we are talking about 0.18ml of insulin is given to [Baby M] as a --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Sorry, 0.18ml of adrenaline is given to [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ah yes, but that would be followed by -- because 0.18ml may just sit in that T-piece, so that has to be followed by a bolus of saline, which is normally -- in a baby of this size is normally 2ml, so that ensures that the adrenaline is pushed through all of that tubing and gets to where it needs to go. So if you just gave 0.18 of a millilitre it would just sit in the tubing.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Because it's not long enough, is it? It has got to be more than the volume of the tube --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it's got to go into the circulation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the tubing is possibly anything from 0.35ml to 0.5ml in volume, something like that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is. I've measured the equipment used in my own unit, but clearly that's not the same as that T-piece, so it would just be an estimate. I think with the three-way tap and a current -- the current octopus that we use, it's about 0.3 of a millilitre.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is it standard to flush the port with saline whenever anything's being put through it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, every port -- yes, any port you would flush before and you flush after.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So if antibiotics are put in, you flush after with saline as well then?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You raised the possibility of what happens with a very small volume of material going into the dead space.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Of course if that's flushed through after the saline that's going to flush it through in any event, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is if it's flushed through, but if it's not and the IV fluids are just reconnected it will go very, very slowly.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But if somebody injects whatever they are injecting into that port, say a course of antibiotics, and then it is flushed with saline, which is what would follow in the course of antibiotics, that flushes it through?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Again, just as you were talking about being difficult to and unable, really, to establish exactly what volume would travel at what speed and in what way, even if we're talking about very small volumes being used, it's impossible to gauge precisely how much would travel how quickly at what rate?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No. But we do know that certainly once we're getting to about 0.3 or 0.4ml, approaching the volume of those tubes, if that's pushed in, that's going to go right the way through?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If it's pushed in, but if it sits in the plastic chamber of the T-piece and the three-way tap and it isn't pushed, but it's just connected to the fluids, it won't be pushed it'll go very, very slowly after that because the rate was 0.8ml per minute.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There's no way of knowing how slowly it would go, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No. Well, only if it's attached to the IV fluids and then we do know how slowly it would go because it would be going at 0.8ml a minute.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But then, as you say, in any event if it was then flushed with saline, that pushes it in in any event?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But why would somebody push saline through afterwards?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: After the use of antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you -- after the use of antibiotics, yes. But not if you've put air in there.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: No, no. I'm just looking at the timings we have and what we've seen on the review, Dr Bohin --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Oh, okay.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- which is antibiotics at 15.45, isn't it, when they were administered?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's the time signed yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Summary of interview with LUCY LETBY re [Baby M] (read)
When interviewed on 5 July 2018, Lucy Letby remembered [Baby M] and the day he collapsed on 9 April 2016 in some detail.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: The nursery had been very busy and he was the fifth baby in nursery 1, which usually only held four babies.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: As a consequence, she said that [Baby M] was attached to a portable Massimo monitor located in a corner space of the nursery, which was not a usual space. He was not on a full Philips monitor.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby recalled the Masimo monitor going off and attended at the monitor. Prior to this, Lucy Letby was checking drugs with Mary Griffith. On hearing the monitor, Lucy Letby went to start an airway for [Baby M] whilst Mary Griffith went for help.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby said that [Baby M] collapsed at about 4 pm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She agreed that she had co-signed for medications at 3.30 and 3.45 pm but was not sure if she had administered them.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: During the interview on 12 June 2019, Lucy Letby repeated that she could remember being in the same room, nursery 1, as the check nurse for medication being prepared by Mary Griffith at the workbench when they heard [Baby M]'s alarm activate. Lucy Letby could not remember if [Nurse B] was in the room at the time and she confirmed that she was, in other words Lucy Letby, the first at his cot side in response and she denied doing anything to harm [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was questioned about the exhibit PMB/8, which are those notes on the paper towel. It was put to her that this was recovered from one of the bedrooms at her home address during a police search. She said that the notes were not all in her handwriting and she thought that she must have taken the paper towel home inadvertently. Lucy Letby could think of no reason why she had kept it but felt that it was an error on her part in not emptying her pockets before leaving work and then inadvertently taking the note home. She said that it may have been put to the side and forgotten about and she denied it was to remind her of an attack on [Baby M].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was shown her diary and she agreed that she had recorded LD for long day and "twins" on 8 April 2016.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She said that she had put that in her diary because she attended the twins' delivery and she had also entered "LD extra twin resus" on 9 April 2016. Lucy Letby said she had documented this as she had done an extra shift and she had documented what had happened that day and she said that the resuscitation was a significant event on that day.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that's very much a short summary of the material that you will receive in due course. I'm not sure we can take it any further today, I'm afraid.
